Let’s dive into Chapter 1: Recognizing the Hidden Rules Shaping Women’s Careers.
Think about this for a moment—what if some of the biggest hurdles you face at work aren’t just about unfair systems or tough bosses, but actually come from habits you picked up long ago?
It’s a quiet realization, but a powerful one.
So many women grow up hearing, “Be nice, be helpful, don’t make waves.” And while those traits can make us really likable in social situations, they can actually get in the way when it comes to building a career.
Here’s something to pay attention to: The expectation to be agreeable often turns into a habit of holding back—whether that’s not speaking up about your needs, not sharing your wins, or hesitating to question authority.
And after a while, these patterns become so automatic, we barely notice them. But they quietly limit what’s possible.
Picture your workplace as a game—a pretty complicated one, with rules nobody ever really writes down.
Some folks are taught to compete, negotiate, and take chances. Others are nudged to keep the peace and go along.
The way we’re conditioned early on can mean our natural instincts don’t always match what actually gets rewarded at work.
Let’s look at a real-world example:
Say there’s someone on your team who always does top-notch work, but she never calls attention to it. She figures, “If I just keep delivering, someone will notice.”
Meanwhile, a colleague who’s more vocal about their achievements gets the recognition—and the promotion.
The lesson? Being visible and speaking up for yourself is just as important as being good at your job.
So, here’s the first big idea: A lot of the behaviors that hold us back aren’t about making bad choices—they’re about following old scripts. These scripts were written by culture, by family, sometimes by school.
Once you start to spot these patterns, you can begin to question them—and even change them.
Let’s talk about some of these unconscious habits that pop up all the time:
Maybe you:
Downplay what you’ve accomplished, or brush off compliments.
Shy away from negotiating, or avoid tough conversations—so you miss out on better pay or new opportunities.
Wait for someone to tell you what to do instead of taking the lead, which can look like you’re not ambitious.
Or, you put everyone else’s needs first and let your own goals slide, which leads to exhaustion or feeling stuck.
Here’s the thing: None of this means you’re lacking drive or talent. It just means you learned to play by rules that don’t always fit the world of work.
There’s a different playbook in the office than there is at home or in school. And real success often means rewriting those old scripts.
So, how do you start?
Try to pay attention to your day-to-day conversations and choices—with a sense of curiosity, not judgment.
Notice if you hold back from speaking up, or feel awkward accepting credit, or squirm when it’s time to advocate for yourself.
Those are signs that old habits might be running the show.
The moment you can name these patterns, you can start to experiment with something different.
This kind of awareness is the foundation.
It sets you up for everything that comes next—like exploring how your words, your body language, and even your tiny, everyday choices can either reinforce those old habits or help you break free from them.
